neighbours.label: bare ' be' as an imperative or hortative ('and be thankful', 'let us be wary', 'be still'), mostly in older literary English; ' be' after a modal stays quiet
fire: Take up your sword, and be brave before the king.
Brothers, let us be glad, for the harvest is in.
Hold your peace, and be content with what you have.
Come, let us be off before the night falls.
Listen well, good sir, and be warned by his fate.
Then, my son, be watchful, for the enemy is near.
Sweet lady, let me be your servant and your friend.
Speak not of it, but be still and wait.
quiet: He took up his sword, and he will be brave before the king.
Brothers, we shall be glad when the harvest is in.
She held her peace and would be content with what she had.
By then they must be off before the night falls.
Good sir, you may be warned by his fate.
My son will be watchful, for the enemy is near.
Sweet lady, I can be your servant and your friend.
They spoke of it, and they should be still and wait.

notes: Probes also fired on 'to be sure' (0.62) and weakly on 'wants to be' (0.24); the top examples include ' to' in 'put to death'. The imperative is the clearest case, not the whole pole.
